title: The first fork: upper or lower motor neuron
description: How tone and reflexes separate an upper from a lower motor neuron lesion, where those rules bend, and how the same reasoning sorts the floppy infant.
why: Deciding whether weakness comes from the upper or the lower motor neuron is the first and most powerful split in localization, and the examination usually makes it within minutes.
objectives: Distinguish upper from lower motor neuron lesions by distribution, wasting, tone and reflexes.
Tell spasticity from rigidity, and place hypotonia on the reflex arc.
Grade reflexes, judge clonus, and recognize a true extensor plantar response at any age.
Recognize when the usual signs mislead: neural shock, early cerebral palsy, axonal Guillain-Barré syndrome, the face.
Decide whether a floppy infant's hypotonia is central or peripheral.

sections.title: Why the two motor neurons fail in opposite ways
sections.content:
Damage the nerve to a muscle and its reflex fades. Damage the pathway from the brain, and the reflex grows livelier. The reason is that every voluntary movement passes through two neurons in series. The **upper motor neuron** runs from the cortex down through the brainstem and spinal cord. The **lower motor neuron** starts in the anterior horn or a cranial nerve nucleus and runs through a root and a nerve to the muscle. The boundary is the synapse on the anterior horn cell (Pearl 2014, p. 65), and lesions on either side of it produce opposite signatures. That makes this the first and most powerful fork in localization.

**Why the signs come out opposite**

The lower motor neuron is the final common path, so when it is cut the muscle loses its nerve supply. It weakens, wastes early and may twitch, and with the reflex arc broken, reflexes and tone fall. The upper motor neuron mostly holds the lower one in check. When it is cut, the surviving lower neuron is **released**, and reflexes and tone rise (Pearl 2014, p. 65).

The two differ under three headings (DeMyer, p. 289).
- **Distribution.** Upper lesions weaken *movements*, in a hemiplegic, quadriplegic or paraplegic pattern. Lower lesions weaken *individual muscles*, or the group served by a root or nerve.
- **Wasting.** Upper lesions cause only slight, late disuse atrophy. Lower lesions cause early, severe denervation atrophy with fasciculations.
- **Reflexes and tone.** Upper lesions bring brisk reflexes, clonus, clasp-knife spasticity and an extensor plantar response. Lower lesions bring reduced or absent reflexes and hypotonia.

> **Bedside trick.** Ask the child to hold both arms out with the palms up and the eyes closed, like a waiter carrying two trays. An arm that turns palm down and sinks is showing pronator drift, a sign of subtle hemiparesis (Pearl 2014, p. 145). It works because upper motor neuron lesions weaken movements, such as a held posture, rather than single muscles (DeMyer, p. 289).

**Try the localizer above.** Switch on brisk reflexes and every level of the motor unit disappears. Switch on absent reflexes and the brain and brainstem disappear, though the spinal cord stays, for a reason section 4 explains.

Two warnings for children follow in sections 4 and 5. An acute upper motor neuron lesion can look floppy, and infant hypotonia is far more often central than peripheral.
keyPoints: The upper motor neuron runs from the cortex to its synapse on the anterior horn cell, and the lower motor neuron runs from the anterior horn to the muscle (Pearl 2014, p. 65).
An upper motor neuron lesion releases the lower neuron, producing brisk reflexes, spasticity, clonus and an upgoing toe.
A lower motor neuron lesion denervates the muscle, producing early wasting, fasciculations, reduced reflexes and hypotonia.
Upper motor neuron lesions weaken movements in hemiplegic, paraplegic or quadriplegic patterns, while lower motor neuron lesions weaken muscles in the pattern of a root or nerve (DeMyer, p. 289).

question.question: A 13-year-old has had six months of weakness in the right hand. The small hand muscles are visibly wasted and twitch with fasciculations, the right triceps and finger reflexes are absent, tone is low, and both plantar responses are flexor. Which side of the first fork does this belong to?
options: An upper motor neuron lesion in the left motor cortex
A lower motor neuron lesion somewhere in the motor unit supplying the right hand
An upper motor neuron lesion in the corticospinal tract of the cervical cord
Neither, because the fork cannot be decided without imaging
question.explanation: Wasting, fasciculations, lost reflexes and low tone in one muscle group are the lower motor neuron signature (DeMyer, p. 289; Pearl 2014, p. 65). A left cortical lesion would weaken the whole arm with brisk reflexes and little wasting, and a cervical cord lesion would make the reflexes brisk, not absent. Imaging comes after localization, and here the examination has already chosen the fork.

sections.title: Tone: spasticity, rigidity and hypotonia
sections.content:
The easiest place to learn normal tone is on yourself. Rest one forearm on your thigh with the wrist dangling, relax it completely, and move the wrist with your other hand. That faint resistance is **tone**, the slight resistance of a relaxed joint to passive movement (DeMyer, p. 270). Every abnormality of tone is a departure from that feeling, and the *kind* of departure is what localizes.

**Spasticity and rigidity, and why speed matters**

The speed of the movement that brings them out tells the two apart (DeMyer, p. 273).
- **Spasticity** appears when you move the limb **quickly**. You feel a catch and then a give, the clasp-knife phenomenon. It follows an upper motor neuron pattern, whether hemiplegic, paraplegic or quadriplegic.
- **Rigidity** is there even when you move the limb **slowly**. The resistance is even through the whole range, like bending a lead pipe, often with cogwheeling and a tremor at rest. It usually affects all four limbs and points to the basal ganglia.

So test tone twice, once slowly and once with a quick flick.

**Hypotonia can arise anywhere along the reflex arc**

Low tone tells you less on its own. Tone depends on a reflex arc from the muscle spindle through the dorsal root to the anterior horn cell and back to the muscle, and a break in any link lets it fall. The signs that come with the low tone tell the peripheral levels apart (DeMyer, p. 266).
- A **dorsal root** lesion lowers tone and reflexes and causes sensory loss, without weakness or wasting.
- A **lower motor neuron** lesion adds weakness, wasting and fasciculations, without sensory loss.
- A **myopathy** gives weakness, wasting and hypotonia, without fasciculations or sensory loss.

:::deeper Why cutting sensory roots relaxes a spastic child
The dorsal root carries the spindle's excitatory signal into the cord, so removing part of that input lowers tone. That is the logic of dorsal rhizotomy, in which selected dorsal roots are cut to reduce tone in some children with spasticity (DeMyer, p. 273).
:::

**In a child**

The term newborn lies flexed, with a tight flexor tone that has eased by about three months ([Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/03month.html)). Hypotonia in an infant is most often **central**, as section 5 shows. Dystonia, a fourth kind of abnormal tone, comes from the basal ganglia and is covered in [[m08-loops|Module 8]].
keyPoints: Tone is the slight resistance of a relaxed joint to passive movement (DeMyer, p. 270).
Spasticity depends on velocity, with a catch and yield on quick movement, and follows an upper motor neuron pattern (DeMyer, p. 273).
Rigidity is present with slow movement as well, as lead-pipe or cogwheel resistance, and points to the basal ganglia (DeMyer, p. 273).
Hypotonia can arise anywhere along the reflex arc, and companions such as sensory loss, fasciculations and wasting tell the levels apart (DeMyer, p. 266).
In infants, flexor tone loosens over the first months, and hypotonia is usually central.

question.question: In a 7-year-old, moving the elbow slowly meets almost no resistance, but a quick extension produces a sudden catch that then gives way. The same arm is weak and its reflexes are brisk. What kind of tone is this, and where does it point?
options: Rigidity, pointing to the basal ganglia
Hypotonia, pointing to the motor unit
Spasticity, pointing to an upper motor neuron lesion
Normal tone in an anxious child
question.explanation: Resistance that appears only with a quick movement and then yields is spasticity, and with weakness and brisk reflexes in the same arm it signals an upper motor neuron lesion (DeMyer, p. 273). Rigidity would be felt on slow movement too. Hypotonia would offer less resistance at every speed. Anxiety can stiffen a limb, but it does not produce a reproducible, speed-dependent catch.

sections.title: Reflexes and the plantar response
sections.content:
How brisk does a reflex have to be before it counts as abnormal? Less hangs on that question than you might expect, because briskness varies and many healthy children have lively reflexes. The reflex hammer tests a circuit from the muscle spindle to the spinal cord and back, which the upper motor neuron holds in check. A **brisk** reflex suggests that restraint has been lost, and an **absent** one suggests the circuit itself is broken. The finding that carries the most weight is **asymmetry** that reappears on repeated testing. Grading reflexes from 0 to 4+ (DeMyer, p. 36) lets you compare findings over time and between examiners. And check for consistency, because an upper motor neuron lesion that brightens the reflexes on one side should also weaken that side (DeMyer, p. 268).

**Clonus**

Clonus is a rhythmic to-and-fro oscillation set off by a quick stretch, another sign of hyperactive reflexes after the upper motor neuron has been interrupted (DeMyer, p. 268). A few beats that die away, called abortive clonus, can be normal, and in mature individuals only **sustained** clonus counts as abnormal. Yet some normal newborns show sustained clonus, set off by movement or by gravity (DeMyer, p. 269), so the sign means different things at different ages.

**What makes a toe "upgoing"**

The extensor plantar response, or Babinski sign, is the most famous sign in neurology and one of the most often misread. A true extensor toe sign has four features (DeMyer, pp. 281-282).
1. The toe begins to extend only after the stroke has traveled some distance along the sole.
2. It stays extended while the stroke continues.
3. When the stroke stops, it floats slowly back to neutral.
4. It comes with a flexion withdrawal of the leg.

There is **no "negative Babinski"**, because the sign is either present or absent (DeMyer, p. 281). Even a true extensor response can be temporary, after a seizure or in toxic-metabolic coma (DeMyer, p. 282).

**In infants**

An upgoing toe is normal in the first year of life, while the corticospinal tracts are myelinating ([Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/newborn_n.html)), and the infant's response varies with the stimulus (DeMyer, p. 282). At 12 months the toe may go either up or down, and what matters then is **reproducible asymmetry** ([Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam](https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/pediatric/html/12month.html)). If the child is ticklish, stroke the outer edge of the foot instead (DeMyer, p. 616).
keyPoints: Grade reflexes from 0 to 4+ (DeMyer, p. 36), and give reproducible asymmetry more weight than absolute briskness.
Brisk reflexes on one side from an upper motor neuron lesion should come with weakness on that side (DeMyer, p. 268).
Only sustained clonus is abnormal in mature individuals, and normal neonates may have sustained clonus (DeMyer, p. 269).
A true extensor toe starts after the stroke has moved, stays up, floats back and comes with flexion of the leg, and there is no such thing as a negative Babinski (DeMyer, pp. 281-282).
An upgoing toe is normal in the first year, and at 12 months it is asymmetry that matters (Utah PediNeuroLogic Exam).

question.question: An anxious 9-year-old's big toe jerks up the instant your key touches the sole, and he pulls his whole foot away, laughing. When you re-test with a slow stroke along the outer edge of the foot, both toes go down. How should you record the plantar responses?
options: Flexor on both sides, because the first response was a withdrawal and not an extensor sign
Extensor on both sides, because the toe went up the first time
Equivocal, with a request for an MRI of the spine
Negative Babinski on both sides
question.explanation: A true extensor toe starts only after the stroke has moved along the sole, stays up and floats back (DeMyer, pp. 281-282). A toe that jerks up at the first touch while the child laughs and pulls away is withdrawal. The re-test from the outer edge of the foot (DeMyer, p. 616) was flexor on both sides, so there is no reason for imaging.

sections.title: When the rules mislead
sections.content:
The upper and lower motor neuron signatures are reliable, but they are not laws. Four exceptions matter most, and three of them matter especially in children.

**1. Shock, an upper lesion that looks lower**

Right after an acute, severe upper motor neuron lesion, the patient may be flaccid and areflexic. This stage is called **neural shock**, spinal or cerebral depending on the site, and brisk reflexes, spasticity and an upgoing toe emerge only as recovery begins (DeMyer, pp. 273-274). In the first days, a child with transverse myelitis or a spinal cord injury can look like a child with a neuropathy. What keeps the cord on your list is the sensory level and the early loss of bladder control (DeMyer, p. 290). Upper motor neuron lesions that evolve slowly skip this floppy phase and are spastic from the start (DeMyer, p. 274).

**2. The floppy infant who will become stiff**

Infants with cerebral palsy may be hypotonic when they first present, before spasticity evolves, and some stay hypotonic (DeMyer, p. 273). Low tone with normal or brisk reflexes, depressed alertness and fairly good limb strength should turn your thinking toward a central cause, as section 5 shows.

**3. A peripheral disorder that keeps its reflexes**

Guillain-Barré syndrome typically brings ascending flaccid weakness with areflexia. In some patients with the axonal form, however, the reflexes are preserved or even brisk. Telling a neuropathy from a myelopathy at the bedside then becomes difficult, and electrodiagnostic studies help to settle it (DeMyer, p. 290).

**4. The face**

Students are taught that a central facial palsy spares the forehead and a peripheral one weakens the whole face. The distinction is useful, but forehead sparing is best treated as a strong hint that falls short of proof.

:::deeper Why the forehead rule leaks
The classic explanation is that the forehead receives input from both hemispheres, so one intact hemisphere is enough to keep it moving. Anatomical studies suggest a gradient instead, in which the forehead receives *less* cortical input rather than more (Pearl 2014, p. 49). The strict version of the teaching therefore overstates the case.
:::

When a single sign contradicts the rest of the picture, ask what could make that one sign misleading before you discard the whole pattern. The usual answers are the time since onset, the age of the nervous system and the kind of axonal injury.
keyPoints: An acute, severe upper motor neuron lesion can be flaccid and areflexic at first, the stage of neural shock (DeMyer, pp. 273-274).
Slowly evolving upper motor neuron lesions show spasticity and brisk reflexes from the start (DeMyer, p. 274).
Infants with cerebral palsy may be hypotonic before spasticity appears (DeMyer, p. 273).
The axonal form of Guillain-Barré syndrome can preserve reflexes, and electrodiagnostic studies help to decide (DeMyer, p. 290).
Forehead sparing in a central facial palsy is a strong hint rather than a law (Pearl 2014, p. 49).

question.question: A 12-year-old woke with weak, floppy legs that worsened over a day. Knee and ankle reflexes are absent, neither big toe moves when the soles are stroked, he cannot feel a pin below the umbilicus, and he has not passed urine since the morning. What is the most likely level?
options: The peripheral nerves, because the reflexes are absent
The spinal cord, in spinal shock
The muscles, because the legs are floppy
Both cerebral hemispheres
question.explanation: Absent reflexes usually point to the motor unit, but a sensory level on the trunk and early urinary retention can only come from the cord. After an acute, severe cord lesion, spinal shock leaves the legs flaccid and areflexic for hours to days (DeMyer, pp. 273-274). Nerve, muscle and hemisphere lesions cannot produce a level on the trunk. This child needs an urgent spine MRI.

sections.title: The floppy infant: central or peripheral?
sections.content:
No problem in child neurology tests the first fork more often than the floppy infant. The evaluation begins with two words that are easy to blur. **Hypotonia** is reduced resistance to passive movement, and **weakness** is reduced maximum power. The two can occur together or apart, and telling them apart is the key to localization ([Peredo 2009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19726697/)).

**Central causes are commoner**

Central causes account for about 60 to 80% of infant hypotonia, and peripheral causes for about 15 to 30% ([Peredo 2009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19726697/)). The floppy infant is therefore more often a brain problem than a muscle problem. That seems backwards at first, until you remember that the motor unit is only one of the places where tone can fail.

**The signs that point centrally**

The features that favor a central cause are a **depressed level of consciousness**, mainly **axial** weakness, **relatively normal limb strength** despite the hypotonia, and **normal or brisk reflexes** ([Peredo 2009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19726697/)). Dysmorphic features, seizures, or poor feeding in a sleepy, disengaged baby add weight. The peripheral pattern is close to the mirror image. The infant is alert and bright-eyed but cannot lift the limbs against gravity, the reflexes are absent, and the tongue sometimes fasciculates.

**The history and examination do most of the work**

About half of infants with hypotonia are diagnosed from the history and examination alone ([Peredo 2009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19726697/)), and the localization chooses the first tests. A central picture calls for brain imaging and genetic testing, and a peripheral one calls for studies of the motor unit.

**One pattern to never miss**

Infant botulism localizes to the neuromuscular junction, and it is treatable. Suspect it in an infant under 6 months who has an acute or subacute floppy illness with constipation, listlessness, poor feeding, a weak cry and a reduced gag ([Peredo 2009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19726697/)).

**Use the presets in the figure above.** The sleepy infant with brisk reflexes leaves the brain and brainstem standing. The alert infant with tongue fasciculations and no reflexes leaves the anterior horn cell on top, which is the picture of spinal muscular atrophy. For the constipated 3-month-old with ptosis and a weak suck, the junction is the only level that fits everything. From there you can follow the trail into the motor unit in [[m04-motor-unit|Module 4]], or into the [neuromuscular disease index](/neuromuscular).
keyPoints: Hypotonia is reduced resistance to passive movement and weakness is reduced power, and the two should be assessed separately (Peredo 2009).
Central causes account for about 60 to 80% of infant hypotonia, and peripheral causes for about 15 to 30% (Peredo 2009).
Depressed consciousness, axial weakness, relatively normal limb strength and normal or brisk reflexes point to a central cause (Peredo 2009).
About half of hypotonic infants are diagnosed from the history and examination alone (Peredo 2009).
Infant botulism should be suspected under 6 months when floppiness comes with constipation, a weak cry, poor feeding and a reduced gag (Peredo 2009).

question.question: A 4-month-old is bright, smiles and follows faces, but cannot lift her arms or legs against gravity. Her reflexes are absent and her tongue quivers at rest. What is the most likely level, and what should happen next?
options: Central hypotonia, so a brain MRI should come first
The neuromuscular junction, so a trial of pyridostigmine is the next step
Muscle, so check the creatine kinase and wait
The anterior horn cell, so arrange urgent genetic testing for spinal muscular atrophy
question.explanation: A bright infant with profound limb weakness, absent reflexes and tongue fasciculations has the peripheral pattern (Peredo 2009), and fasciculations with areflexia point to the anterior horn cell. That is spinal muscular atrophy, whose treatments are time-sensitive, so genetic testing should be urgent. Central hypotonia would come with sleepiness and preserved reflexes, and junction and muscle disorders do not cause fasciculations.

quiz.question: Which combination of findings most strongly suggests a lower motor neuron lesion?
options: Weakness of a hand, early wasting, fasciculations and an absent reflex
Weakness of the whole arm, brisk reflexes and an upgoing toe
Lead-pipe rigidity in all four limbs
Ataxia with normal strength
quiz.explanation: Early wasting, fasciculations and a lost reflex in a group of muscles are the lower motor neuron signature (DeMyer, p. 289). Weakness of the whole arm with brisk reflexes and an upgoing toe is the upper motor neuron picture. Lead-pipe rigidity points to the basal ganglia, and ataxia with normal strength to the cerebellum, so neither implicates the motor neurons.

quiz.question: A 16-year-old has brisk reflexes in the right arm and leg. On careful testing the right side is not weak at all, and on re-examination the reflexes on the left are just as brisk. How should you interpret the reflexes?
options: A left hemisphere lesion
A cervical cord lesion
Probably physiological briskness, since re-testing shows no asymmetry and there is no matching weakness
A peripheral neuropathy
quiz.explanation: Reflex briskness varies among healthy people, so what matters is asymmetry that can be reproduced. Brisk reflexes on one side from an upper motor neuron lesion should come with weakness on that side (DeMyer, p. 268). Symmetric brisk reflexes without weakness are usually physiological, and a peripheral neuropathy lowers reflexes rather than raising them.

quiz.question: Testing a 10-year-old's ankle, you feel four beats of clonus that then stop. The other ankle behaves the same way, and there is no weakness. How should this be recorded and interpreted?
options: Sustained clonus, indicating corticospinal tract disease
Unsustained (abortive) clonus, which can occur in normal individuals
A sign of spinal cord compression requiring urgent imaging
A sign of peripheral neuropathy
quiz.explanation: A few beats that die away are abortive, or unsustained, clonus, which can occur with physiological hyperreflexia. In mature individuals only sustained clonus counts as abnormal (DeMyer, p. 269). With no weakness and no asymmetry there is no reason to suspect cord compression, and a neuropathy reduces reflexes and does not cause clonus.

quiz.question: A 2-month-old is floppy, feeds poorly and is hard to rouse, yet moves the limbs against gravity, and the reflexes are brisk. Which level of the nervous system is most likely involved?
options: The anterior horn cell
The peripheral nerves
The muscle
The brain (central hypotonia)
quiz.explanation: Depressed consciousness, fairly preserved limb strength and normal or brisk reflexes are the features of central hypotonia, which accounts for most hypotonia in infants (Peredo 2009). Disorders of the anterior horn cell, nerves and muscle look different, with an alert infant, true weakness and reduced reflexes. Brain imaging and genetic testing come first here.

quiz.question: A 4-year-old has a right facial palsy in which he cannot close the right eye fully or wrinkle the right forehead, and the right arm and leg are normal. How confident can you be that this is a peripheral (lower motor neuron) facial palsy?
options: Fairly confident, since whole-face weakness with normal limbs favors a peripheral lesion, though forehead involvement is a hint rather than a law
Certain, because the forehead is always spared in central palsies
Not at all, because the face cannot be localized at the bedside
It must be central, because the eye is involved
quiz.explanation: Weakness of the whole face, forehead included, with normal limbs is the usual picture of a lower motor neuron facial palsy. But forehead sparing in central palsies is not absolute, because the forehead may receive less cortical input rather than more (Pearl 2014, p. 49). The finding supports the localization without proving it, and weak eye closure does not make a palsy central.

signOff: On five patients, classifies the weakness as upper or lower motor neuron from the examination alone, agreeing with faculty.

opener.parable: Stroke the sole of a four-month-old's foot and the big toe will often rise, which is entirely normal at that age. Do the same in a four-year-old and the identical movement tells you that something has gone wrong in the pathway coming down from the brain.
opener.history: In 1896 Joseph Babinski (1857–1932) described the big toe that rises instead of curling when the sole is stroked after damage to the upper motor neuron. He also introduced the word anosognosia, for a patient with a left hemiplegia who seemed unaware of it.
